title: All the Matches of the League
statement:
A league is described by a single table:

- `Teams(team_name)`: one row per team; `team_name` is unique.

Every team plays every other team exactly twice: once as the home side and once as the away side. A team never plays itself.

List every match of the season with the columns `home_team` and `away_team`. Rows may come in any order.
constraints: A team never plays against itself
reference:
SELECT home.team_name AS home_team, away.team_name AS away_team
FROM Teams AS home
JOIN Teams AS away
  ON away.team_name <> home.team_name;
brute:
SELECT a.team_name AS home_team, b.team_name AS away_team
FROM Teams AS a, Teams AS b
WHERE a.team_name < b.team_name
UNION ALL
SELECT b.team_name, a.team_name
FROM Teams AS a, Teams AS b
WHERE a.team_name < b.team_name
notes:
## Intuition

A match is an **ordered** pair of different teams: who plays at home and who travels. Pairing every row of `Teams` with every row of `Teams` (a self-join) produces all ordered pairs, including each team paired with itself; dropping those self-pairs leaves exactly the season's fixtures. Because the pair is ordered, (A, B) and (B, A) are both kept, which gives each pair of teams its two meetings.

## Approach

1. Read `Teams` twice: alias `home` for the home side and `away` for the visitors.
2. Join them on `away.team_name <> home.team_name`, which pairs each team with every other team and never with itself.
3. Select the two names as `home_team` and `away_team`.

## Example 1, step by step

With three teams there are 3 × 3 = 9 ordered pairs. The three self-pairs (Leetcode FC vs Leetcode FC, and so on) fail the `<>` condition, leaving 6 matches:

| home_team | away_team |
| --- | --- |
| Leetcode FC | Ahly SC |
| Leetcode FC | Real Madrid |
| Ahly SC | Leetcode FC |
| Ahly SC | Real Madrid |
| Real Madrid | Leetcode FC |
| Real Madrid | Ahly SC |

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²) for n teams, which is unavoidable since the output has n · (n − 1) rows.
- Space: O(n²) for the result.

## Pitfalls

- A plain `CROSS JOIN` without a condition also reports each team playing itself.
- Using `<` instead of `<>` keeps only one of the two meetings of every pair.
- Swapping the aliases in the select list still gives a correct set, but naming the columns anything other than `home_team` and `away_team` fails the check.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `home` | `Teams` as the home side of a match |
| `away` | `Teams` as the visiting side |
| `ON away.team_name <> home.team_name` | pairs each team with every other team, never itself |

narration.1: Name the two sides of each match home_team and away_team.
narration.2: The first copy of Teams supplies the home side.
narration.3: Join a second copy of Teams for the visiting side.
narration.4: Any two different teams form a match; requiring different names removes a team playing itself.
